  • Does the size of an ovarian cyst determine treatment?
Family Health

Does the size of an ovarian cyst determine treatment?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Size matters when an ovarian cyst is assessed, but it is only one part of the decision. A measurement makes most sense alongside the scan appearance, the type of cyst suspected and how you are feeling.

Read the measurement alongside the scan description

An ovarian cyst is a sac on or within an ovary. Some contain clear fluid; others contain blood, thicker material or tissue. Most are benign, particularly before menopause, but the word cyst alone does not tell you which type is present.

A report may give several dimensions in millimetres or centimetres. Ten millimetres equals one centimetre, so a measurement of 50 mm is 5 cm. Ask about both the largest dimension and the appearance: a thin-walled, fluid-only cyst is different from a mass with solid components.

Size contributes to the decision, together with symptoms, changes over time, age, menopausal status and pregnancy or fertility plans. There is no single measurement that automatically proves a cyst is harmless, cancerous or in need of surgery.

Functional cysts arise around ovulation

A follicle is the small fluid-containing structure in which an egg develops. A follicular cyst can form when the follicle does not release its egg and continues to enlarge. After ovulation, the remaining structure becomes the corpus luteum; fluid or blood can collect within it and form a corpus luteum cyst.

These functional cysts are related to the menstrual cycle. Many cause no symptoms and resolve over several weeks or menstrual cycles. They are not the same as dermoids, cystadenomas or endometriomas, which have different origins.

A normal follicle near ovulation may measure roughly 2–3 cm. Calling every structure of that size a disease is misleading. Functional cysts are often only a few centimetres, but a larger persistent finding needs its own assessment rather than a presumed functional label.

Why a list of typical sizes can mislead

Ranges such as 2–5 cm or reports of functional cysts reaching 8–12 cm are not boundaries that diagnose the type. A cyst does not become functional simply because its diameter falls within a quoted range. Its appearance and whether it resolves are also informative.

Unit conversions can make a large difference to how a report sounds. Two to five centimetres is about 0.8–2 inches, not two to more than three inches. Use the actual scan measurement and units rather than an approximate comparison found elsewhere.

A small suspicious mass can require investigation, while a larger, clearly characterised simple cyst may sometimes be monitored. That does not mean that every simple cyst up to 10 cm can safely be left alone.

Dermoid cysts contain different types of tissue

An ovarian dermoid, usually a mature cystic teratoma, develops from germ cells and may contain fat, hair or other mature tissues. It is generally benign and can be found during the reproductive years. Its developmental origin does not establish that a visible ovarian cyst has necessarily been present since birth.

Some dermoids remain symptom-free for a long time. Larger lesions can cause pressure or contribute to complications such as twisting of the ovary. Occasionally very large dermoids, including those exceeding 15 cm, are reported, but an extreme example is not the expected course for everyone.

The scan pattern, symptoms and interval change matter more than comparing your measurement with a photograph or a dramatic case report.

Dermoid growth figures need a study attached

The often-quoted growth rate of about 1.8 mm a year comes from a 1997 study of small dermoids. It followed 72 people before menopause and 14 after menopause, all with cysts under 6 cm at entry. The premenopausal average was 1.77 mm per year. An average from that selected group is not a forecast for an individual cyst.

A later two-case report estimated much faster growth, about 8 and 25 mm per year, after masses became visible on later imaging. Those estimates were based on intervals between scans, including earlier CT studies without a visible mass; they were not continuous measurements of a known cyst.

The cases show that a benign dermoid can be considered even when apparent growth is faster. They do not make rapid growth reassuring or remove the need for review. They also do not establish an 8–25 mm yearly range that every dermoid will follow.

Cystadenomas can persist and become large

Cystadenomas are usually benign ovarian tumours that can contain watery or mucus-like fluid. A fluid-filled one may initially resemble a simple cyst on ultrasound, but unlike many functional cysts, it may persist and enlarge rather than disappear with subsequent cycles.

Some are only a few centimetres. Rare examples can grow much larger, including around 30 cm. A measurement of 1–3 cm should not itself be described as very large, and a maximum reported size is not a threshold to wait for before seeking care.

Persistent growth is a reason to revisit the assessment. Imaging can suggest the likely type, but definitive classification sometimes requires examination of removed tissue.

Endometriomas are linked with endometriosis

Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining outside its usual location. When it affects an ovary, a cyst containing old, dark blood can develop. This is an endometrioma, sometimes called a chocolate cyst because of its contents.

Published estimates often cited in patient information suggest that about 17–44% of people with endometriosis have an endometrioma. The denominator matters: this is not the proportion of all women with an ovarian cyst, and estimates depend on the population studied.

Endometriomas vary in size and can be associated with pelvic pain, painful periods, pain during sex or difficulty conceiving. Having one does not by itself mean that pregnancy is impossible.

Symptoms may involve pressure, pain or bleeding changes

Many cysts are discovered incidentally. When symptoms occur, they can include one-sided lower abdominal pain, a dull ache or sharper discomfort, pelvic pressure, fullness, bloating or visible swelling.

Other possible complaints include painful sex, painful or irregular periods, bleeding between periods, needing to urinate more often, or difficulty emptying the bladder or bowels. These symptoms are not unique to ovarian cysts, so an incidental cyst should not automatically be blamed for everything.

Mention persistent symptoms, changes in bleeding and any possibility of pregnancy when seeking assessment. The clinician can decide whether examination, ultrasound or other testing is needed.

Sudden severe symptoms need urgent assessment

A cyst can rupture and cause pain or bleeding. An ovary can also twist around its supporting tissues, a condition called torsion, which can threaten its blood supply. Although these complications are uncommon, a previously reassuring scan should not delay help for new severe symptoms.

Seek urgent care for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, especially with nausea, vomiting or fever. Severe pain with fainting, marked weakness or rapid, shallow breathing needs emergency assessment. Do not wait for a routine repeat scan.

These symptoms can have other urgent causes too. If pregnancy is possible, say so immediately; having a known cyst does not rule out a pregnancy-related emergency.

Size bands are specific to the situation

RCOG’s older premenopausal patient leaflet gives examples for painless simple cysts: below 5 cm often needs no treatment, 5–7 cm may be followed by ultrasound, and above 7 cm may prompt additional imaging or surgery. These examples are not a universal operation rule at 5–6 cm.

After menopause, the pathway differs. RCOG’s December 2025 update says a simple cyst up to 3 cm, on one side and with a single compartment, does not require routine follow-up. That advice should not be extended to a symptomatic, complex or poorly characterised mass.

Your clinician should apply the relevant current local pathway. Ask which features place your cyst in a monitoring or referral category, rather than treating one size band as a substitute for the full assessment.

Monitoring and relief of discomfort

Watchful waiting is an active plan: it may include a repeat scan to see whether the cyst resolves, changes or persists, together with instructions about symptoms that should prompt earlier contact. The interval depends on the type and circumstances; it is not always exactly one or two cycles.

For mild discomfort after assessment, a clinician may suggest acetaminophen, also called paracetamol, or sometimes an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen or naproxen. Suitability depends on pregnancy, other medicines and medical history. These are pain-relief options, not cyst-dissolving treatments.

Do not assume an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory is safe during pregnancy. The FDA warns against self-use of NSAIDs at around twenty weeks or later. Get individual medicine advice and do not mask escalating pain while postponing assessment.

When surgery or hormonal treatment may be discussed

Surgery may be considered for a persistent or enlarging cyst, significant symptoms, a complication or features concerning for cancer. Ultrasound can identify suspicious features, but it does not by itself establish the final tissue diagnosis.

Many operations use laparoscopy, with small abdominal incisions. An open operation may be recommended for a very large mass or concern about malignancy. Discuss whether the plan is to remove the cyst alone, when an ovary might need removal, and the potential effect on fertility.

Endometrioma surgery deserves particular discussion about ovarian reserve. ESHRE does not recommend routinely removing an endometrioma before assisted reproduction solely to improve live-birth chances; pain, access to follicles and other findings may change the decision.

Hormonal contraception can sometimes reduce new functional cyst formation, but should not be promised to shrink a cyst already present. A Cochrane review of eight trials found no faster resolution with combined oral contraceptives, a distinction also retained in ASRM guidance. Treatment should match the reason it is being offered.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A diameter alone does not determine the diagnosis or the need for surgery.

Functional cysts, dermoids, cystadenomas and endometriomas have different behaviour.

How BeMama can help

Keep the scan report and ask what type is suspected, which features matter, when to repeat imaging and what symptoms should prompt earlier help.

When to seek help

Sudden severe pelvic pain, especially with vomiting, fever or faintness, needs urgent assessment. Severe pain with collapse or signs of shock is an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check whether the measurement is in millimetres or centimetres.
  • Simple-cyst monitoring rules do not apply to every mass.
  • Growth averages and rare giant cysts are not personal predictions.
  • Persistent symptoms and changing scan features deserve review.
  • Birth-control pills do not reliably make existing functional cysts resolve faster.

Frequently asked questions

Does a 5 cm cyst automatically need surgery?

No. Symptoms, appearance, type and life stage affect the decision as well as size.

Is a 2–3 cm follicle always an abnormal cyst?

No. A follicle of that size can be part of ovulation; the scan needs clinical interpretation.

How many inches is a 2–5 cm measurement?

Approximately 0.8–2 inches. The original scan units are the clearest reference.

Will every dermoid grow 1.8 mm each year?

No. That figure is an average from a selected older study, not an individual forecast.

Does rapid growth always mean cancer?

No, but it needs assessment. A small case series of benign dermoids does not make all rapidly growing masses safe.

Does the 17–44% endometrioma estimate apply to all women?

No. It is a reported range among people with endometriosis and varies by study population.

Can a small simple cyst after menopause be left without routine scans?

In some circumstances, yes. The updated RCOG recommendation applies to a specific simple-cyst pattern; your clinician should confirm that it fits.

Can ultrasound prove a mass is cancerous?

It can show concerning features and guide referral, but the final diagnosis may require further assessment and tissue examination.

Will the contraceptive pill shrink my current functional cyst?

It has not been shown to speed resolution. Preventing new cysts is a separate possible purpose.

Can I wait for my follow-up if I develop sudden severe pain?

No. Seek urgent care, especially with vomiting, fever, weakness or faintness.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
